ambiguous.why: Modern ransomware is usually double-extortion (exfiltrate then encrypt), so a practitioner could read the primary loss as confidentiality; the item text mentions only encryption, and the hint steers to availability, so availability is the intended answer.

Immutability is often taught as an integrity control; the availability reading depends on treating the backup copy as the restore path. The prompt's 'reachable through any disruption' framing makes IN the stronger answer.

ambiguous.item: Separation of duties on payment approvals
ambiguous.why: Where separation of duties is enforced by workflow software it can be argued as a technical control; as a stated organisational rule about who may approve what, it is administrative, which is the standard CC treatment.

ambiguous.item: You refuse to scan a network you have no written authorisation to test
ambiguous.alternative: Canon I — protect society and the infrastructure
ambiguous.why: Unauthorised scanning is both illegal conduct (II) and a threat to the common infrastructure (I); the item is framed around your own legality, so II is the better fit, but I is defensible.

ambiguous.item: You tell a client up front that a specialised cloud engagement is beyond what you are qualified to deliver
ambiguous.alternative: Canon II — act honourably, honestly, justly, responsibly and legally
ambiguous.why: This is an act of personal honesty as much as a duty owed to a principal. Canon III's 'render only services for which you are qualified' language makes III the intended answer, but the honesty reading is defensible.

ambiguous.item: You decline to exaggerate a threat in a sales pitch to frighten a prospect into buying
ambiguous.alternative: Canon IV — advance and protect the profession
ambiguous.why: FUD-based selling damages the profession's standing, so IV is arguable; the item centres on your own truthfulness towards a prospect (not yet a client), so II is the primary reading.

ambiguous.item: Every system must have a named owner who is accountable for its security
ambiguous.why: It is mandatory and uniformly applied, so it can read as a standard; it states an accountability principle with no technology or configuration detail, which puts it in the policy layer.

ambiguous.item: To report a suspected phishing email, click Report, then forward it to the security inbox
ambiguous.why: It lacks the numbered-step form of the other procedure item and could be read as user guidance, but it prescribes an ordered sequence of actions, which is a procedure.

misleading_hints.hint: Ask two questions: is it mandatory, and does it name specific technology or specific steps?
misleading_hints.why: It collapses standards and procedures into one test outcome — 'specific technology' and 'specific steps' are the distinguishing features of two different layers, so a learner applying the hint to 'Step 1: open the admin console...' can land on Standard.
